question.text: XYZ Financial Services wants to become the sponsor of a new mutual fund. The company has been in financial services for 7 years. It has maintained positive net worth in six of the last seven years; the one exception was a year of negative net worth that occurred 4 years ago. Its average net annual profit over the past 5 years is Rs. 12 crore. Is XYZ eligible to sponsor a mutual fund?

answer.text: Yes, because the company meets the experience, profit, and current net worth criteria
Yes, because having positive net worth in 6 of the last 7 years exceeds the minimum requirement
No, because the sponsor must have positive net worth in ALL of the immediately preceding five years, and one of those five years was negative
No, because the minimum average net profit required is Rs. 15 crore, not Rs. 12 crore

explanation.text: The Logic: Apply each sponsor-eligibility criterion independently. (1) At least 5 years in financial services: MET (7 years). (2) Positive net worth in ALL of the immediately preceding five years: NOT MET — a negative net worth year occurred 4 years ago, which falls inside the immediately preceding 5-year window. (3) Average net annual profit of at least Rs. 10 crore over the immediately preceding 5 years: MET (Rs. 12 crore exceeds the Rs. 10 crore floor on p.63). (4) Fit-and-proper status: assumed met. Because criterion (2) explicitly requires ALL five years to be positive, a single negative year inside that window disqualifies the applicant. The Trap: Option A is the tempting wrong choice because three of four criteria are clearly met. Option B mis-states the rule as "6 of 7 years" — there is no "most years" averaging provision; the regulation reads ALL five immediately preceding years. Option D invents an Rs. 15 crore floor; the workbook floor is Rs. 10 crore on p.63. In the audit-flagged original wording, the scenario said "positive net worth for 6 consecutive years" while also saying net worth was negative 4 years ago — internally inconsistent over a 7-year history, which let candidates argue either way. Note: The original scenario was internally contradictory ("six consecutive years positive" plus "negative four years ago" cannot both be true). The wording has been rephrased to "positive net worth in six of the last seven years; the exception was four years ago", which preserves the intended test of the p.62 rule (positive net worth in ALL immediately preceding five years) while removing the contradiction. Source: NISM Series V-A workbook, pp.62-63.
